title: Guanyin
hookLine: in China, Avalokiteshvara becomes Guanyin, the one who hears the cries of the world

lines: A WHITE FIGURE ABOVE THE SEA.
cards: A white figure stands on a rock above the sea, or sits on a lotus, a small vase tipped in one hand. She's in temples and taxi cabs, on kitchen shelves and in restaurant corners, in China and well beyond it.
Fishermen have called on her in storms. Mothers have called on her at bedsides.
Trace her back far enough, past the white robes and the vase, and you arrive at an Indian bodhisattva this path has already met, shown in India as a man, with a long Sanskrit name: Avalokiteshvara.

teach.b: The Lotus Sutra has a chapter given over to this bodhisattva, and in China it was copied, chanted and carried on its own. In it, the Buddha is asked why the bodhisattva has this name.
His answer is the heart of today: when beings in any kind of trouble call the name with one mind, the bodhisattva perceives the sound of their voices, and they are set free.
Fire, flood, shipwreck, a raised sword, chains: the chapter goes through them one by one.

In Chinese the name became Guanshiyin, shortened to Guanyin, and it carries that scene inside it: the one who perceives the sounds of the world. Not the one who rules it or judges it. The one who hears.
The same chapter says the bodhisattva takes whatever form will help the one who is suffering: a monk, a king, a child, a woman.
In China, over time, Guanyin came to be pictured more and more as a woman, robed in white, gentle and near.
Some Chinese stories give her a human life, like the tale of Princess Miaoshan, who gave her own eyes and arms to heal the father who had rejected her.
People who love Guanyin hold both: the Indian bodhisattva of the sutra and the mother figure of the shrine.
And a bodhisattva whose whole name is listening says something about compassion.
Before it fixes anything, it hears. It turns toward the sound instead of away from it.

how: Across East Asia, Buddhists call on Guanyin by name, keep her image at home and in temples, and chant the Lotus Sutra's chapter on the bodhisattva, often called the Universal Gate chapter.

games.q: in the Lotus Sutra, someone asks the Buddha why this bodhisattva bears this name. what's the answer?
o: because the bodhisattva rules the world.
because the bodhisattva hears those who call.
because the bodhisattva was a princess.
games.why: when beings in trouble call the name with one mind, the bodhisattva perceives the sound of their voices, and they are freed.

practice: For a minute, just listen to the sounds around you, near and far, a hum, a voice, your own breath, and let each one arrive without sorting it into good and bad.
Then bring to mind one person whose voice you've only half heard lately, and in your mind, turn fully toward them.

wordCard.voice: Guanyin. The Chinese name for Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva who perceives the sounds of the world and answers in whatever form will help.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the bodhisattva's Indian name, known in China as Guanyin.

carryVoice: Your line: she hears the cries. Compassion starts by turning toward the sound. See you tomorrow.
